pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years (KS1)

- **Topic:** The Heart & Blood — the heart is a muscle that pumps blood around the body through tubes (blood vessels); you can feel your heartbeat at your chest and pulse points

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1, Animals including humans):** at KS1 the statutory content is the basic needs of animals including humans for survival (water, food and air) and the importance of exercise; the heart-as-pump is TOPICAL/enrichment framing at this age (the circulatory system is formalised at Y6: 'identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system, and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood'). Honest note: there is no KS1 statutory 'heart pumps blood' line — treat this as an age-appropriate first encounter that seeds Y6.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** nearest is K-LS1-1 (what animals need to survive); the circulatory system as an interacting subsystem lands formally at MS-LS1-3. So at age 5–7 this is enrichment on both sides, not a graded standard.

- **Operational details:** Keep it embodied and concrete — the whole point at KS1 is that the heart is REAL, inside YOU, and working right now. Three ideas: (1) the heart is a MUSCLE that squeezes (pumps) over and over, never stopping; (2) it pushes BLOOD through tubes called blood vessels that reach every part of the body — fingertips, toes, everywhere; (3) you can FEEL the pump as a heartbeat (hand on chest) or a pulse (fingers on wrist/neck), and it speeds up when you run or jump. Anchor every abstract claim in a felt experience: make a fist to show its size, squeeze a soft ball to 'be' the pump, find your own pulse, then run on the spot and feel it race. Correct the cartoon heart early — the real heart is a fist-sized muscle slightly left of centre, not the ❤ symbol. Avoid the blue-blood trap: blood is always red (bright red when full of oxygen, darker red when not) — veins only LOOK blue through the skin.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, embodied). Success = locate own heartbeat/pulse by touch, say the heart pumps blood continuously, and describe blood vessels as tubes carrying blood to every part of the body. Depth stops at 'pump + tubes + you can feel it' — chambers and the double loop are Y6, not now.
bestPractices: Anchor every claim in an embodied action — make a fist for size, squeeze a ball to be the pump, find a pulse, run and feel it race — so the heart is felt, not just told.
Correct the cartoon-heart image explicitly: the real heart is a fist-sized muscle roughly centre-left of the chest, not the ❤ shape.
Head off the blue-blood misconception from the start — blood is red; veins only look blue through skin.
Link heartbeat speed to activity (rest vs running) to make the pump's job — delivering to working muscles — intuitive without formal detail.
Use the tube/network image (vessels reach everywhere) rather than any chamber detail; keep the depth at KS1 level and let Y6 add structure.
Use simple, consistent language: 'pump', 'squeeze', 'blood vessels are tubes' — avoid arteries/veins/capillaries naming at this age.
keyRepresentations: A fist held up to show the heart's real size and location (centre-left of chest)
A soft squeeze-ball as a stand-in pump the child works with their hand
Pulse points (wrist, neck) the child presses to feel the beat
A simple body outline with tubes (vessels) branching to hands, feet and head
A rest-vs-running heartbeat comparison (slow thump → fast thump)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the heart is shaped like the ❤ symbol, rather than a fist-sized muscle.
Believing the heart is on the far left edge of the chest rather than roughly centre-left.
Thinking blood is blue inside the body and turns red only in air — blood is always red.
Believing the heart only 'beats' with emotions (love/fright), not that it pumps blood every second of life.
Thinking blood just sits still in the body or only appears when you are cut, rather than constantly circulating.
Confusing the heartbeat with breathing, or thinking the heart and lungs are the same thing.

learn.summary: KS1 (ages 5-7) first encounter with the heart and blood: the heart is a fist-sized muscle, roughly centre-left of the chest, that pumps (squeezes) blood continuously through tubes called blood vessels to every part of the body, and you can feel this pumping as a heartbeat (hand on chest) or pulse (fingers on wrist/neck), which speeds up with activity. Keep depth at 'pump + tubes + you can feel it'; chambers and the double circulation are later content (the circulatory system is introduced from Year 6, and the detailed structure of the heart is often taught later still). This is enrichment, not a graded KS1/early-elementary standard. Activities are embodied and concrete, anchoring every abstract claim in a felt experience, and explicitly correct the valentine-shape, far-left-placement, blue-blood, 'heart only beats with emotions/only beats when you move', 'blood only where you are cut', and heart-is-the-same-as-lungs misconceptions.

activities.title: Be the heart: pump blood around the body
feedback: If a child says the heart stops or rests when sitting still: have them feel the pulse while sitting completely still to prove it is beating now - it speeds up when you run but never stops.
If a child thinks blood only appears where you are cut: trace the tubes reaching the hands and feet and point out blood is travelling everywhere all the time.
Reinforce that blood is always red - bright red when carrying lots of oxygen, darker red when carrying less; it only looks blue through the skin.
Praise locating the pulse by touch and saying 'the pump I feel is my heart moving blood around me'.
activities.rationale: At KS1 the single felt idea - the heart is a real muscle inside you, pumping blood continuously - is intended to be built mainly by doing and feeling, with telling in a supporting role. Pairing a driveable pump with the child's own synced pulse can tie the invisible internal process to a felt, controllable cause and effect. An optional on-screen 'be the heart' model (each tap squeezes out a pulse of red blood, a wrist dot throbs in time, a 'go for a run' button makes the body call for more blood so the child pumps faster) can make 'the heart never stops' and 'it races when you run' concrete; a squeeze-ball offers the same mechanism tactilely.
sourceClaims: The heart is a muscular pump about the size of a fist, located slightly left of centre in the chest; a pulse felt at the wrist/neck reflects each heartbeat, and heart rate rises with physical activity.
learnerActions: Make a fist and hold it to the centre-left of your chest to show how big your real heart is and where it sits.
Squeeze a soft ball (or tap/press a beating heart on screen) over and over, never stopping, to 'be' the pump.
Watch or imagine each squeeze pushing a pulse of red blood out along the tubes (blood vessels) to the hands, toes, and head, then looping back for the next squeeze.
Place two fingers on your own wrist or neck and find the beat; notice it throbs in time with each pump.
Pretend to go for a run (run on the spot), then feel your pulse again and notice it is faster - the working muscles are asking for more blood, so the heart pumps faster.
activities.intendedInsight: The heart is a never-stopping muscle that squeezes blood through tubes to every part of the body right now; the beat you feel at your wrist is that pump working, and it speeds up when you are active.

activities.title: Find it, name it, bust the myths: a body you can explore
feedback: If a child picks the valentine symbol as the real heart: explain the symbol is just a picture people use; the real heart is a lumpy fist-sized muscle that squeezes blood.
If a child places the heart at the far-left edge: correct gently to roughly centre-left of the chest.
If a child says blood turns red only in air: blood is always red - bright red when carrying lots of oxygen, darker red when carrying less; it only looks blue through the skin.
Confirm correct pulse-point finds and correct vessel tracing to hands and feet.
activities.rationale: Locating the heart and pulse and busting the shape and colour myths directly target documented KS1 misconceptions and build the vocabulary (pump, squeeze, blood vessels are tubes) without introducing arteries/veins/capillaries or chambers. A tap-to-reveal body illustration with a 'not this heart-symbol' myth-buster flap and a lift-the-flap 'is blood blue? -> always red!' is an optional way to make the reveals concrete; this is a scaffold for locating and naming and does not by itself convey the continuous pumping motion.
sourceClaims: The heart is a muscular pump about the size of a fist, located slightly left of centre in the chest; a pulse felt at the wrist/neck reflects each heartbeat, and heart rate rises with physical activity.
learnerActions: On a body outline (or your own body), point to where the real heart is - centre-left of the chest, about the size of your fist.
Compare the real fist-sized heart muscle with the valentine heart symbol and say which one is the real organ and what the real one does.
Find the pulse points at the wrist and neck by pressing gently with two fingers (on one side of the neck only).
Trace the tubes (blood vessels) branching out to the hands, feet and head to show blood reaches everywhere.
Answer 'is blood blue?' and give the correct answer: blood is always red; veins only look blue through the skin.
activities.intendedInsight: The heart is a fist-sized muscle (not the valentine shape) sitting centre-left; blood is always red and travels through tubes to every part of the body, and you can find your pulse where those tubes run near the skin.

activities.title: Ask the heart: why do you pound when I run?
feedback: Prompt the child to connect the faster beat to the running, not just to name it.
If the child says the heart stops when resting, return to feeling the pulse while sitting still.
Celebrate explanations that use 'pump', 'squeeze' and 'blood vessels are tubes'.
activities.rationale: A short spoken, responsive exchange after the hands-on model lets the child articulate and may consolidate what they discovered by doing. Its narrow affordance is eliciting explanation in the child's own words; it is intended to follow, not replace, the feeling and doing that the embodied activities are designed to build at this age.
learnerActions: Talk with a friendly cartoon heart or school nurse: first find your own pulse, then say what you feel.
Jump or run on the spot, feel your pulse again, and describe out loud what changed.
Explain back, in your own words, why the heart beats faster when you run (the muscles are working harder and need more blood).
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the felt experience into your own words - the pump speeds up when your body works harder - can consolidate that the heart responds to what your body is doing.

activities.title: Quick checks: real heart, pulse points, always pumping
feedback: For the two-cuts question, confirm both bleed because blood vessels carry blood to every part of the body - blood is everywhere, not only where you are cut.
Reinforce 'the heart keeps pumping even when you sleep' as true - it never stops.
Use any wrong answer as a cue to return to feeling the pulse or tracing the vessels, not just to mark it wrong.
activities.rationale: Picture-based recognition and simple true/false items verify the core facts at an age-appropriate level, and the two-cuts prompt pushes the child to state the 'blood is everywhere' idea rather than assume it. These recognition items check what a child can identify; they do not require the child to independently construct or demonstrate the pumping action, so pair them with the hands-on activities rather than relying on them alone.
learnerActions: Choose the real heart from two pictures (fist-sized muscle vs the valentine symbol).
Tap or point to where you can feel a pulse.
Answer true/false: 'the heart keeps pumping even when you are asleep.'
Answer: if you got a tiny cut on your finger and on your toe, would both bleed? Why?
activities.intendedInsight: Checking the basics confirms the child can recognise the real heart, knows where to feel a pulse, and can state that the heart pumps blood everywhere, all the time.

constraints: Keep depth at 'pump + tubes + you can feel it': do not introduce heart chambers, the double circulation, or arteries/veins/capillaries naming at KS1 - these belong to later study (the circulatory system is introduced from Year 6, and the detailed structure of the heart is often taught later still).

This topic is enrichment, not statutory/graded at this age: UK KS1 statutory content is the basic needs of animals (water, food, air) and the importance of exercise, with the circulatory system formalised at Year 6; the nearest US standard is K-LS1-1 (what animals need to survive), with the circulatory system as an interacting subsystem treated at MS-LS1-3.
Use simple, consistent language: 'pump', 'squeeze', 'blood vessels are tubes'.

Keep blood-colour language accurate: blood is always red, bright red when carrying lots of oxygen and darker red when carrying less; do not say blood is 'full of air' or that it turns red only in air.

Explicitly correct the valentine-shape, far-left-placement, blue-blood, 'heart only beats with emotions', and 'blood only where you are cut' misconceptions, and distinguish the heartbeat from breathing (heart and lungs are not the same thing).

Anchor every abstract claim in a felt action (fist for size, squeeze-ball or screen pump, finding a pulse, running and feeling it race); do not rely on telling alone, though telling in a supporting role is valuable.
Recognition-only check items verify identification and do not elicit independent construction of the pumping idea; use them alongside the embodied activities, not as a replacement.

The tap-to-reveal body and the dialogue are scaffolds for locating/naming and for consolidating; they do not by themselves build the felt understanding of continuous pumping. This does not mean telling or dialogue cannot contribute to learning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source notes honestly that there is no KS1 statutory 'heart pumps blood' line and treats this as an age-appropriate first encounter seeding Year 6; two of the three sources (NGSS and BHF) are marked verified:false in the row.

The original row framed the driveable 2D model as uniquely able to convey continuous pumping and rated a 3D model 'poor' as adding nothing; these are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy/necessity claims. They have been softened to scoped proposals - a squeeze-ball or screen pump each make the mechanism concrete in different ways - without asserting one medium is necessary or that other media cannot teach the idea.

Candidate phrasing 'blood full of air' was corrected to 'carrying oxygen' to avoid reinforcing an air-in-blood confusion; 'blood is always red' is retained as an accurate KS1 simplification, with richer arterial/venous oxygenation detail intentionally omitted as beyond-age.
Near-categorical modality phrasing in the pump and dialogue rationales was scoped with 'intended to/can/may' wording; efficacy of these specific activities is untested.

Independent re-audit confirmed the prior blood-colour and modality corrections are present at every learner-facing occurrence, and additionally scoped one remaining efficacy claim ('ties' -> 'can tie') in the first activity's rationale.

probeDeeper: Put two fingers on your neck or wrist and stay very still — can you feel a beating? What is that?
If your heart stopped beating for a while, why would that be dangerous — what does the blood do for your body?
Can you find any part of your body that has NO blood in it at all? Where?
assess.correctAnswer: The heart is beating and blood is moving all the time, even sitting still — it beats faster when you run but never stops. Both the finger and the toe bleed because blood travels through tubes (blood vessels) to every part of the body, so blood is everywhere, not only in one spot and not only when you exercise.

errorPatterns.pattern: The heart only beats and blood only moves when you run or move about.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Feel the pulse while sitting still to prove it beats now; explain it speeds up with exercise but never stops.
errorPatterns.distractor: It only beats when you run — when you sit still it stops.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the heart rests or stops when sitting still.

errorPatterns.pattern: Blood is only in the place where you get cut / not spread all through the body.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the two-cuts evidence: both bleed because vessels carry blood everywhere; trace vessels reaching hands and feet.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only the finger would bleed, because that's where the blood is.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects only the finger to bleed; treats blood as localised.

errorPatterns.pattern: The heart is for feelings or love (the valentine shape) rather than a pump for blood.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the everyday 'heart' symbol from the organ; the real heart is a muscle that pumps blood.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the heart's job as holding feelings, not pumping blood.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the heart beats only during exercise, or that blood is only where you bleed / appears only when cut.
responseLevels.full: States the heart beats and blood flows all the time (faster when active) AND that blood travels through vessels to every part of the body, using the two-cuts evidence to justify it.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the heart pumps blood but is unsure it happens continuously, or that blood reaches every part — holds one idea but not both.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Right now, sitting still, is your heart beating and is your blood moving — or does that only happen when you run around? And if you got a tiny cut on your finger AND on your toe, why would BOTH bleed? What does that tell you about where your blood is?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the heart rests when still, or that blood sits in one place, gives the wrong answer to at least one half. Only a child who holds 'always pumping' AND 'blood everywhere' answers both, and the two-cuts evidence in tier two forces the 'blood is everywhere' idea to be stated, not assumed.
